title: Roots, factors and irreducibles
objectives: Use the factor theorem and test small polynomials for irreducibility.

screens.title: Where the curve crosses
screens.prose: The curve is $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Drag each point along it to a root, where $f(x) = 0$.
screens.question: Drag A, B and C to the three roots, in order from left to right.

hints.text: A root is where the curve meets the x-axis.
The curve crosses at whole numbers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put each point where the curve meets the x-axis.

byKey.p1: A is off. The leftmost crossing is at $x = 1$.
byKey.p2: B is off. The middle crossing is at $x = 2$.
byKey.p3: C is off. The rightmost crossing is at $x = 3$.

explain.text: $f(1) = 1 - 6 + 11 - 6 = 0$, and likewise $f(2) = f(3) = 0$. So $f$ has three roots. Next we see what a root says about factors.

screens.title: Divide by x minus a root
screens.prose: Divide $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6$ by $x - 1$, as in l16. The table runs the division with coefficients only.
screens.question: What is the remainder?

hints.text: Each entry is the one above plus 1 times the entry to its left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Finish the last column: $-6 + 1 \times 6$.

byKey.const: You took the constant term of $f$. The remainder is $-6 + 6$ after the last step.

explain.text: The remainder is 0, and $f = (x - 1)(x^2 - 5x + 6) = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)$. In l16, dividing $x^3 - 2x^2 - 4$ by $x - 3$ left 5. That is $27 - 18 - 4 = 5$, the value at 3.

screens.title: The factor theorem
screens.prose: The **factor theorem**: over a field, $f(a) = 0$ exactly when $(x - a)$ divides $f$. The remainder on dividing by $x - a$ is always $f(a)$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Divide: $f(x) = q(x)(x - a) + r$ with $r = 0$ or $\deg r < 1$ (division algorithm, l16).
Substitute $x = a$: $f(a) = q(a) \cdot 0 + r = r$ (evaluation keeps $+$ and $\times$).
So $f(a) = 0$ exactly when $r = 0$, that is, when $(x - a)$ divides $f$.

lines.why: You dropped the remainder. At $x = a$ the term $q(a)(a - a)$ is 0, leaving $r$.

hints.text: The remainder has degree below 1, so it is a constant.
Put $x = a$ to read off $r = f(a)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by $x - a$, then substitute $x = a$.

byKey.d1: You lost $r$. At $x = a$ the product $q(a)(a - a)$ vanishes and $r$ remains.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: $f(x) = q(x)(x - a) + r$, with $r$ a constant. At $x = a$ this gives $f(a) = r$. So $f(a) = 0$ exactly when $x - a$ is a factor.

screens.title: At most d roots
screens.prose: Claim: a non-zero polynomial of degree $d$ over a field has at most $d$ roots. Induct on $d$; degree 0 is a non-zero constant, with no roots. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the inductive step in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\deg f = d \ge 1$. If $f$ has no root we are done; else let $a$ be a root (cases).
$f = (x - a)q$ with $\deg q = d - 1$ (factor theorem; degrees add in a field).
If $b$ is another root, $0 = f(b) = (b - a)q(b)$ (substitute).
$b - a \ne 0$ and a field has no zero divisors, so $q(b) = 0$ (l15).
So the roots of $f$ are $a$ and roots of $q$: at most $1 + (d - 1) = d$ (induction hypothesis).
A root $b$ of $f$ gives $b - a = 0$ or $q(b) = 0$, in any ring.
lines.why: Not in any ring: in $\mathbb{Z}_8$, $(3 - 1)(3 + 1) = 8 \equiv 0$ with neither factor 0.

hints.text: Split off one root with the factor theorem.
No zero divisors gives $q(b) = 0$; then use the hypothesis on $q$.

feedback.correct: Right. The field's lack of zero divisors drives the count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Factor out $x - a$, then show every other root is a root of $q$.

byKey.d1: You used the zero product rule in any ring. It fails in $\mathbb{Z}_8$, which is why $x^2 - 1$ has four roots there.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: A root $a$ splits $f = (x - a)q$. Any other root $b$ has $(b - a)q(b) = 0$, so $q(b) = 0$ in a field. So $f$ has at most $1 + (d - 1) = d$ roots.

screens.title: Too many roots
screens.prose: $\mathbb{Z}_7$ is a field, and $x^2 - 1$ has the two roots 1 and 6 there. $\mathbb{Z}_8$ is not a field. The table gives $x^2 \bmod 8$.
screens.question: Which $x$ are roots of $x^2 - 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_8$? Select all that apply.

feedback.correct: Right. Four roots for a degree 2 polynomial.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every $x$ with $x^2 \equiv 1$.

explain.text: 1, 3, 5 and 7 all square to 1 mod 8. Degree 2 with four roots is possible because $\mathbb{Z}_8$ has zero divisors: $(3 - 1)(3 + 1) = 8 \equiv 0$. Over the field $\mathbb{Z}_7$ there are only two.

screens.title: Small degrees: roots decide
screens.prose: $f$ is **irreducible** over $\mathbb{F}$ when it is not a product of two polynomials of lower degree. For degree 2 or 3, a root decides the question. Order the two halves.
screens.question: Prove: $f$ of degree 2 or 3 over $\mathbb{F}$ is reducible exactly when it has a root.

lines.text: If $f = gh$ with $\deg g, \deg h \ge 1$, then $\deg g + \deg h = \deg f \le 3$ (degrees add in a field).
So one factor is linear, $cx + e$ with $c \ne 0$, and $-e/c$ is a root of $f$ (field: divide by $c$).
Conversely, a root $a$ gives the factor $x - a$, of lower degree (factor theorem).

hints.text: Split $\deg f \le 3$ into two positive parts.
A linear factor gives a root, and a root gives a linear factor.

feedback.correct: Right. For degree 2 or 3, no root means irreducible.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from a factorisation and look at the degrees.

explain.text: Two positive degrees summing to 2 or 3 include a 1. A linear factor $cx + e$ gives the root $-e/c$. So degree 2 or 3 is irreducible exactly when there is no root.

screens.title: One polynomial, three fields
screens.prose: The table gives $x^2 + 1$ at each element of $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $\mathbb{Z}_3$ and $\mathbb{Z}_5$. By the last screen, a root decides irreducibility.
screens.question: How many roots does $x^2 + 1$ have in each field?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the zeros in each row.

byKey.double: You counted 1 twice. $x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$: one root, repeated.

explain.text: Over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2$ has the one root 1. Over $\mathbb{Z}_3$ there is no root, so it is irreducible. Over $\mathbb{Z}_5$ it is $(x - 2)(x - 3)$.

screens.title: Real root, still irreducible
screens.prose: Over $\mathbb{Q}$, the rational root test says a root $\tfrac{u}{v}$ of $x^3 - 2$ in lowest terms has $u \mid 2$ and $v \mid 1$. So the candidates are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 2$.
screens.question: Is $x^3 - 2$ irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$?

options.text: Yes. No candidate is a root, and degree 3 with no rational root is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
No. It has the real root $\sqrt[3]{2}$, so it factors.
options.why: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is not rational. Over $\mathbb{Q}$ the factors must have rational coefficients.

options.text: No. Every cubic has a root, so every cubic factors.
options.why: Every real cubic has a real root, but not always a rational one. Here none is rational.

options.text: We cannot tell without trying every rational number.
options.why: The rational root test limits the candidates to four, and all four fail.

hints.text: Degree 3 with no root in $\mathbb{Q}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

feedback.correct: Right. Irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, though not over $\mathbb{R}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the four candidate values.

explain.text: None of $\pm 1, \pm 2$ is a root, so $x^3 - 2$ has no rational root. Degree 3 with no root is irreducible. Over $\mathbb{R}$ it factors, since $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is real.

screens.title: No roots, yet it factors
screens.prose: $x^4 + 4 \ge 4$ for every real $x$, so it has no rational root. The plane also draws $x^2 + 2x + 2$ and $x^2 - 2x + 2$.
screens.question: Is $x^4 + 4$ irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$?

options.text: No. $(x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2) = x^4 + 4$, two factors of degree 2.
Yes, since it has no root.
options.why: You used the root test past degree 3. A quartic can split into two quadratics without any root.

options.text: Yes, since it is positive on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
options.why: Positivity rules out roots, not factors. Both quadratic factors are positive too.

options.text: No, it has the factor $x + 2$.

feedback.correct: Right. No roots does not mean irreducible at degree 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand the product of the two quadratics.

byKey.yes: You used the root test at degree 4. It only works for degree 2 or 3; $x^4 + 4$ splits into two quadratics.

explain.text: $(x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2) = (x^2 + 2)^2 - 4x^2 = x^4 + 4$. Neither factor has a real root, so neither does the product. The root test decides only degrees 2 and 3.

screens.title: The Sicherman dice
screens.prose: A classic interview puzzle. Over $\mathbb{Q}$, $x + \dots + x^6 = x(1 + x)(1 + x + x^2)(1 - x + x^2)$, all irreducible. Regroup the square into $x(1 + x)(1 + x + x^2)$, faces 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, and $x(1 + x)(1 + x + x^2)(1 - x + x^2)^2$. The bars show both pairs of dice.
screens.question: Expand $x(1 + x)(1 + x + x^2)(1 - x + x^2)^2$. Its exponents are the second die's faces; give them in increasing order.

hints.text: The product is $x + x^3 + x^4 + x^5 + x^6 + x^8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply out, and read the exponents with coefficient 1.

explain.text: The product is $x + x^3 + x^4 + x^5 + x^6 + x^8$, so the faces are 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8. Its product with the first die is $(x + \dots + x^6)^2$ again. A market maker pricing a bet on the sum cannot tell the two pairs apart.

screens.title: Roots by search
screens.prose: Write `roots_mod(f, p)`, the sorted roots in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of a coefficient list (lowest first). Then `irreducible_small(f, p)` for degree 2 or 3, by roots; raise `ValueError` for any other degree. Trying every residue proves the answer for that one field.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 9 hidden tests: eight results compared exactly, and one degree-4 call that must raise ValueError.

hints.text: Try every x in range(p), not only 0 and 1.
Find the degree after dropping zero top coefficients.
Raise ValueError unless the degree is 2 or 3.

feedback.correct: Right. And the degree-4 case refuses, as the trap requires.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Search all of $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and refuse degrees other than 2 and 3.

explain.text: `roots_mod` tries all $p$ residues, which settles the question in $\mathbb{Z}_p$. `irreducible_small` is only valid at degree 2 or 3. At degree 4, $x^4 + x^2 + 1 = (x^2 + x + 1)^2$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ has no root but factors.

ideas: Factor theorem: dividing by $x - a$ leaves $f(a)$, so $f(a) = 0$ exactly when $x - a$ divides $f$.
Over a field, degree $d$ means at most $d$ roots, since there are no zero divisors. In $\mathbb{Z}_8$, $x^2 - 1$ has four.
Degree 2 or 3 is irreducible exactly when there is no root. At degree 4 check quadratic factors: $x^4 + 4 = (x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2)$.

formula.name: Factor theorem
formula.note: Over a field: the remainder on dividing by $x - a$ is $f(a)$.

summary.trap: Calling a quartic irreducible because it has no root: $x^4 + 4$ and $x^4 + x^2 + 1$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ both factor.

quiz.prose: In $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $x^3 + x + 1$ takes the values 1, 1 at $x = 0, 1$. In $\mathbb{Z}_5$ it takes 1, 3, 1, 1, 4 at $x = 0$ to 4.
quiz.question: What can we conclude?

options.text: It is irreducible over both $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_5$: degree 3 and no root.
Irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ only.
options.why: No value in $\mathbb{Z}_5$ is 0 either, so it has no root there.

options.text: Nothing, since roots never decide irreducibility.
options.why: For degree 2 or 3 they do: a factorisation needs a linear factor.

options.text: It is reducible, since it has degree 3.
options.why: Degree alone decides nothing. A cubic with no root has no linear factor.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a 0 among the values.

explain.text: No value is 0, so there is no root in either field. A reducible cubic would have a linear factor and so a root. So $x^3 + x + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_5$.

quiz.prose: Over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ there are $p^2$ monic quadratics $x^2 + bx + c$. The reducible ones are $(x - u)(x - v)$: $p$ with $u = v$ and $\tfrac{p(p-1)}{2}$ with $u \ne v$.
quiz.question: How many monic irreducible quadratics are there over $\mathbb{Z}_5$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the reducible ones from $p^2 = 25$.

byKey.all: You counted every monic quadratic. Remove the 15 reducible ones.
byKey.red: You gave the reducible count, $5 + 10 = 15$. The question asks for the rest.

explain.text: Reducible: $5 + \tfrac{5 \times 4}{2} = 15$. So $25 - 15 = 10$ are irreducible, matching $\tfrac{p^2 - p}{2}$. For $p = 2$ and 3 the formula gives 1 and 3.

quiz.prose: Over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, both $x^4 + x^2 + 1$ and $x^4 + x + 1$ take the value 1 at 0 and at 1, so neither has a root.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: $x^4 + x^2 + 1 = (x^2 + x + 1)^2$ factors; $x^4 + x + 1$ is irreducible.
Both are irreducible, since neither has a root.
options.why: You used the root test at degree 4. $(x^2 + x + 1)^2 = x^4 + x^2 + 1$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

options.text: Both factor into two quadratics.
options.why: The only irreducible quadratic over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ is $x^2 + x + 1$, and its square is $x^4 + x^2 + 1$.

options.text: $x^4 + x + 1$ factors; $x^4 + x^2 + 1$ is irreducible.
options.why: You swapped them. Square $x^2 + x + 1$ mod 2 to see which one appears.

feedback.correct: Right. At degree 4, check quadratic factors too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square $x^2 + x + 1$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

explain.text: $(x^2 + x + 1)^2 = x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x + 1 \equiv x^4 + x^2 + 1$. That is the only product of two irreducible quadratics over $\mathbb{Z}_2$. So $x^4 + x + 1$ is irreducible.

quiz.prose: Constants are units or 0, and every linear polynomial is irreducible. $x^2 + x + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
quiz.question: How does $\mathbb{F}_4$ from l15 arise?

options.text: As $\mathbb{Z}_2[x]$ modulo $x^2 + x + 1$, with $\alpha$ the class of $x$, so $\alpha^2 = \alpha + 1$.
As $\mathbb{Z}_4$.
options.why: $\mathbb{Z}_4$ has $2 \times 2 = 0$; it is not a field.

options.text: As $\mathbb{Z}_2[x]$ modulo $x^2 + 1$.
options.why: $x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ is reducible, so that quotient has a zero divisor.

options.text: As $\mathbb{Z}_2[x]$ modulo $x + 1$.
options.why: Dividing by a linear polynomial gives a copy of $\mathbb{Z}_2$, with two elements.

feedback.correct: Right. An irreducible quadratic makes a field of size $2^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the irreducible quadratic over $\mathbb{Z}_2$.

explain.text: Working in $\mathbb{Z}_2[x]$ with $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$ leaves four remainders $0, 1, x, x + 1$. Calling $x$ by the name $\alpha$ gives $\alpha^2 = \alpha + 1$. That is $\mathbb{F}_4$.
